lessons.title: Designing a mixed crop and livestock system
lessons.html:
Designing a mixed crop and livestock system

A mixed farm combines crops and livestock so that each supports the other. In South Africa, examples include maize and beef cattle in the Free State and Mpumalanga, wheat and sheep in the Swartland and Overberg, and smallholder systems with maize, vegetables, goats and poultry in Limpopo and the Eastern Cape.

Why integrate?

  • Nutrient cycling: manure returns nutrients and organic matter to cropland, reducing fertiliser costs.
  • Feed from crops: crop residues (maize stover, wheat stubble), planted pastures and grain feed livestock, especially in winter when veld quality is low.
  • Risk spreading: a drought, price collapse or disease in one enterprise is buffered by the other.
  • Labour and machinery use spread more evenly across the year.
  • Rotations: pasture phases improve soil structure and break pest and weed cycles.

Matching enterprises to resources

ResourceQuestions to ask
Climate and rainfallSummer or winter rainfall? Reliability? Frost?
SoilsDepth, texture, potential for cropping versus grazing only
VeldGrazing capacity, condition, sweetveld or sourveld
WaterBoreholes, dams, irrigation rights
MarketsSilo, abattoir, auction, feedlot, fresh produce market distance
Capital and skillsMachinery, handling facilities, management experience

Arable land with good soils is normally used for crops, while shallow, rocky or steep land stays under veld for grazing. The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 controls the cultivation of virgin land and the protection of soil, vegetation and wetlands, so land-use decisions must comply with it.

The farm plan

A whole-farm plan maps camps, lands, water points and infrastructure, sets enterprise sizes, and shows the annual calendar of planting, harvesting, calving, lambing, weaning and marketing so labour and cash flow can be planned.

lessons.title: Managing crop and livestock enterprises together
lessons.html:
Managing crop and livestock enterprises together

Crop enterprise management

  • Choose cultivars suited to the area and planting window.
  • Base fertiliser on soil analysis and yield targets.
  • Plan rotations, for example maize followed by soya or a pasture phase.
  • Use integrated weed, pest and disease management.
  • Plan harvest, storage and marketing before planting.

Livestock enterprise management

  • Set the stocking rate to the grazing capacity of the veld and pastures, not to the number of animals you would like to keep.
  • Plan breeding seasons so calving or lambing matches feed availability.
  • Follow a herd health programme with your vet: vaccination, parasite control, record keeping.
  • Keep production records: weaning weights, calving percentage, mortality.

Linking the two

LinkManagement point
Crop residuesGraze stover after harvest, but leave enough cover to protect soil
Planted pasturesUse in rotation; fertilise and rest according to the species
ManureCollect from kraals or pens and apply to lands; avoid run-off to water
Grain on farmFeed own maize to animals when market price is low
Fodder conservationMake silage or hay for the dry season

Planning the feed flow

A fodder flow plan compares monthly animal feed requirements with what veld, pastures, residues and conserved fodder can supply. Gaps, usually in late winter, must be filled by planted fodder, purchased feed or by reducing animal numbers in time.

Records and decisions

Gross margin per enterprise, per hectare and per large stock unit shows which enterprises earn their place. Review records every season and adjust enterprise mix.

Key points

  • Integration cycles nutrients, uses residues and spreads risk.
  • Match enterprises to climate, soils, veld, water and markets.
  • CARA (Act 43 of 1983) governs cultivation and resource protection.
  • Stock to grazing capacity and plan fodder flow for the dry season.
  • Use gross margins to compare and adjust enterprises.
